title: Conservation and dissipation of energy

assemble.prompt: Match each term to its definition.

items.label: Wasted energy
items.clue: The everyday name for energy that has been dissipated.

items.label: Energy efficiency
items.clue: The share of the energy supplied to a device that is transferred usefully.

items.label: Lubrication
items.clue: Putting a substance such as oil between surfaces that move over each other.

items.label: Conservation of energy
items.clue: Energy can be transferred usefully, stored or dissipated, but it cannot be created or destroyed.

questions.stem: A torch is left switched on until its battery is flat. What has happened to the energy that was in the chemical store of the battery?

options.text: It has been transferred to light and to thermal stores, so the total is unchanged.
It has slowly been used up, so there is less energy now than at the start.
The part of it that was wasted has been destroyed inside the torch.
It is stored in the bulb and is released again when the torch cools.

questions.explanation: Energy cannot be created or destroyed; it has been transferred usefully and dissipated, leaving the total the same.

questions.stem: A small electric motor is supplied with 800 J of energy. Of this, 260 J is transferred usefully to a kinetic store. What is the efficiency of the motor?
questions.explanation: efficiency = (useful output energy transfer)/(total input energy transfer) = 260 J / 800 J = 0.325.

questions.stem: A ball bearing rolls along a bench and slowly comes to rest. The ball, the bench and the surrounding air are treated as a closed system. What is true of the total energy of this system?

options.text: It has fallen, because friction has let some of the energy leak out of it.
It has fallen, because energy was used up in slowing the ball down.
It is unchanged; the kinetic store has emptied into the thermal stores.
It has risen, because the friction has created extra thermal energy.

questions.explanation: In a closed system there is no net change to the total energy; the energy has only moved between stores inside it.

questions.stem: Which statement about the efficiency of a device is correct?

options.text: A very well made device can have an efficiency of more than 1.
The efficiency of a device can never be greater than 1.
Efficiency is measured in joules when energy values are used.
Efficiency gives the fraction of the input energy wasted.

questions.explanation: The useful output energy transfer cannot exceed the total input energy transfer, so the ratio is at most 1.

questions.stem: In every system change some of the energy is dissipated. What does dissipated mean?

options.text: The energy is stored in the surroundings and later returns to the system.
The energy is stored in less useful ways, usually in thermal stores.
The energy is shared out equally between all the stores in the system.
The energy is destroyed as it spreads out into the surroundings.

questions.explanation: This is what the specification means by dissipation: energy ends up in stores that cannot do the intended job.

questions.stem: A motor has a total power input of 1200 W and a useful power output of 900 W. What is the efficiency of the motor?
questions.explanation: efficiency = (useful power output)/(total power input) = 900 W / 1200 W = 0.75, a ratio with no unit.

questions.stem: A food mixer is running. Which energy transfer in the mixer is best described as ‘wasted’?

options.text: The transfer to the kinetic store of the rotating blades.
The transfer that is destroyed by friction in the bearings.
The transfer to the room that flows back into the mixer later.
The transfer to the thermal store of the warm motor.

questions.explanation: Energy that warms the motor is dissipated: it is stored in a less useful way and cannot turn the blades.

questions.stem: The bearings of a machine are oiled regularly. Why does this reduce the unwanted energy transfers?

options.text: The oil takes in the wasted energy and stores it so it can be used again.
There is less friction, so less energy is dissipated to the thermal stores.
The oil removes the friction entirely, so no energy is dissipated.
The oil makes the moving parts lighter and so easier to turn.

questions.explanation: Lubrication lowers the friction between the moving surfaces, so a smaller share of the input is dissipated.

questions.stem: Thick insulation is laid in the loft of a house. Which statement about the house is now correct?

options.text: No energy can leave through the loft now, so the house never cools.
The insulation gives out warmth of its own and heats the rooms up.
The building now cools down more slowly than it did before.
The energy is destroyed inside the insulating material.

questions.explanation: The insulation lowers the rate of energy transfer through the loft, so the building cools more slowly.

questions.stem: Two saucepan handles are the same size and shape, but one is made from a material with a higher thermal conductivity than the other. Which statement about that handle is correct?

options.text: It transfers energy by conduction at a higher rate than the other one.
It transfers energy more slowly, because it holds the energy inside itself.
It transfers energy at the same rate, as the handles match in size.
It must be thicker in order to conduct energy at that rate.

questions.explanation: The higher the thermal conductivity of a material, the higher the rate of energy transfer by conduction across it.

questions.stem: Two houses are identical except that one has thicker outside walls, built from the same brick. On a cold night, compared with the other house, the house with the thicker walls will

options.text: cool down faster, because there is more brick that has to be warmed up.
cool at the same rate, because the brick has the same conductivity.
warm itself up, because the thick walls give energy to the rooms.
cool down more slowly than the house with thinner walls.

questions.explanation: For the same material, a thicker wall gives a lower rate of energy transfer, so the building cools more slowly.

questions.stem: An architect wants a new building to cool down as slowly as possible on a cold night. Which change should be made to its walls?

options.text: Build them from a material that has a higher thermal conductivity.
Make them thinner so that less brick has to be warmed up first.
Make them thicker and use a material of lower thermal conductivity.
Make them thinner and choose a brick that conducts more quickly.

questions.explanation: Both factors act the same way: greater thickness and lower thermal conductivity each lower the rate of cooling.

questions.stem: (HT) A gearbox wastes energy because of friction between its moving parts. Which change would increase the efficiency of the intended energy transfer?

options.text: Lubricate the moving parts to reduce the energy dissipated.
Supply more power to the gearbox, so that it does more work each second.
Remove the friction completely so the gearbox is 100% efficient.
Run the gearbox for less time, so that less energy is wasted overall.

questions.explanation: Reducing an unwanted transfer leaves a larger share of the input as useful output, which raises the efficiency.
